sentences.text: Its known jaw fragments measure only a few centimeters, leading to an estimated total skull length of roughly 7.6 centimeters.
Like modern birds, this animal possessed three fingers on each hand and the same number of toes on its feet, with bones fused in a similar manner.
This species holds the distinction of being the oldest known oviraptorosaur that lacked teeth in its lower jaw.
Estimates suggest the creature grew to about two feet in length and weighed approximately three pounds.
The species Caenagnathasia martinsoni was formally named and described in 1994 by Philip J. Currie, Stephen Godfrey, and Lev Nessov.
The specific name honors the paleontologist Gerbert Genrikhovich Martinson.
The genus relies on a holotype consisting of a pair of fused lower jaw bones, alongside a second specimen referred to the species.
The dentary bone lacked teeth, a feature that distinguishes it as the earliest oviraptorosaur with this characteristic.
Specimens made up mainly of lower jaws were initially assigned to birds by researchers Sternberg in 1940 and Cracraft in 1971.
While some suggest it might hold a more basal position in Oviraptorosauria outside Caenagnathoidea, it is generally considered a basal member of the family Caenagnathidae.
Following the description of new material in 2015, scientists concluded that the animal could confidently be referred to the family Caenagnathidae.
This dinosaur lived at the end of the Cretaceous period, specifically during the Turonian stage around 92 million years ago in what is now Asia.
It is speculated that Caenagnathasia lived near the time when the family Caenagnathidae and Oviraptoridae separated.
